title: The ring in the meadow
teaches: A mushroom is only the fruit of a hidden net of threads; a fairy ring is one fungus spreading outward for centuries
summary: **A mushroom is a fruit.** The fungus that makes it is a net of threads, the mycelium, living out of sight in soil, litter or wood.
**Each thread is a hypha.** Hyphae are a few thousandths of a millimetre across, and a gram of rich soil can hold metres of them.
**A fairy ring is one fungus growing outward.** It starts from a single point and spreads evenly in every direction while the soil allows.
**Mushrooms come up only at the edge.** That is where the fungus is reaching fresh food; the ground behind it is used up.
**The grass shows the fungus's work.** A lush band where the fungus frees nitrogen, often a dead band where its dense threads keep water out, and recovery behind.
**Rings that meet both stop.** Neither fungus can grow into soil the other has used, which Wollaston noticed in 1807.
**A ring's width dates it.** At a few tens of centimetres a year, a ring tens of metres across has been growing for a century or more.

blocks.text: On old pasture, chalk downland and lawns that nobody has dug for a long time, the grass sometimes grows in a ring. The ring might be two metres across or two hundred. Its edge is a band of grass darker and thicker than the rest, and inside that band there is often a second band where the grass is thin, yellow or dead. In late summer and autumn a ring of small tan mushrooms comes up along the edge, sometimes so evenly spaced that it looks laid out with a compass.

People have explained these rings in many ways. In English and Dutch folklore they were where fairies or witches danced at night, and stepping inside one was unlucky. Other explanations were more practical: lightning striking the ground in a circle, moles running in a ring, a haystack once standing there, the urine of cattle tethered to a post. The rings were also known to move. A farmer who looked at the same field year after year could see them grow wider, as if something under the grass were spreading out from the middle.

The mushrooms were the clue, and the question was which way round the connection ran. Did something in the soil make a ring, and the mushrooms come up where conditions suited them? Or were the mushrooms the visible part of the thing making the ring?

William Hyde Wollaston was a London physician who gave up medicine for chemistry. He found the elements palladium and rhodium, worked out how to make platinum into wire and sheet, and made a fortune from it. He was also a careful walker. In 1807 he read a short paper to the Royal Society, *On Fairy-Rings*, describing what he had seen on the grass downs.[^withering]

Wollaston noticed three things. The mushrooms always grew at the outer edge of a ring, never in the middle. The rings grew wider every year. And where two rings ran into each other, they did not cross. Both stopped at the meeting place, and the arcs where they touched faded out.

His explanation was that a ring is a fungus that uses up something it needs from the soil. It starts at a point and spreads, and because the soil behind it is exhausted, it can only go outward, so it forms an ever-widening circle. Two rings cannot cross because each would have to grow into soil the other had already used. Later work filled in what was being used up and what the fungus does to the grass, but his picture has held.

blocks.caption: A fairy ring seen from above, spreading year by year. Each square is a metre. A model with one rule: a fungus can only grow into soil no fungus has used.
blocks.task: Let a second ring start nearby and run the years until they meet

blocks.text: In the model a single rule is enough to make both the ring and the way rings meet. Nothing tells the fungus to make a circle. It simply grows outward at about the same speed in every direction, because the conditions are about the same in every direction, and it cannot go back.

The fairy-ring mushroom, *Marasmius oreades*, is a small pale-brown cap on a tough stem. Pull one up and it seems to be all there is. It is not. Under the turf the soil is threaded through with fine white filaments, so dense in a band under the ring's edge that the soil looks mouldy and smells of mushrooms. Those filaments are the fungus. The mushroom is only its fruit, put up for a few days to scatter spores, the way an apple tree puts up apples.

blocks.caption: An apple is the fruit of a tree; a mushroom is the fruit of a fungus. The tree is mostly above ground. The fungus is almost all below, as a spreading net of threads, drawn here far thicker than life.

blocks.text: Each filament is a **hypha** (plural hyphae), a tube a few thousandths of a millimetre across, about a tenth the width of a human hair. A mass of hyphae is a **mycelium**. Hyphae are too thin to see one at a time, but where they are crowded you can see the mycelium as a white web in leaf litter or a felt under a rotting log. Rich forest soil can hold metres of hyphae in a single gram.[^length] The mushroom itself is built of the same hyphae, packed tightly into the shape of a stem, a cap and gills.

This is the first thing to know about fungi, and the rest of the course rests on it. What we notice, a mushroom, a bracket on a tree, a puff of green mould on bread, is usually a brief and small part of a living thing that is long-lived, large and almost invisible. Most fungi never make a mushroom at all.

Behind its front, the fungus is feeding. The fairy-ring fungus lives on dead plant matter in the turf: old roots, fallen leaves, the thatch at the base of the grass. It digests them, which the next lessons explain, and in doing so it releases nitrogen that was locked up in them, as ammonium. Grass is often short of nitrogen, so where the fungus has just been at work the grass greens up and grows thick. That is the dark band at the edge.

Just behind the front, where the mycelium is densest, the grass may die. The tight mat of hyphae repels water: the soil there stays dry even after rain, and the grass roots go thirsty.[^dry] Further in, the old mycelium dies back, the soil wets again, and the grass recovers. Some rings show all three bands, some only the green one, and some show nothing at all until the mushrooms come up.
So the rings in the grass are a map of the fungus underground. A dark band is where it is feeding now, a dead band is where it is thickest, and the plain grass inside is where it used to be.

Because a ring grows at a fairly steady rate, its size gives its age. The fairy-ring mushroom spreads somewhere between about 10 and 35 centimetres a year, depending on the soil and the weather. A ring 10 metres across, growing 20 centimetres a year at its edge, has a radius of 5 metres and so has been growing for about 25 years.

Rings tens of metres across are not rare on old grassland. Several in Europe are well over a hundred metres across, and one in eastern France is said to be about 600 metres across and several hundred years old.[^france] A ring that size has grown through the lives of many generations of farmers, which is why a field's rings could be part of local lore. The fungus behind the oldest of them is among the oldest living things in its landscape.

Few rings stay perfect for that long. A path, a tree, a patch of different soil or another fungus breaks the circle into arcs, and the arcs carry on outward on their own. Each arc is still the same individual fungus, and the next lessons begin with how it grows.

blocks.caption: Five questions on rings and mycelium
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: What is a mushroom, in relation to the fungus that makes it?
choices: Its fruit, a short-lived part for scattering spores
The whole fungus, which lives only a few days
A separate organism that feeds on the fungus
items.why: The fungus is the mycelium, a net of hyphae in the soil or wood. A mushroom is built of the same hyphae, packed together for a few days to release spores.

items.ask: Why do the mushrooms of a fairy ring stand only at its outer edge?
choices: The fungus is reaching fresh food only at the edge
The middle is too shaded by the grass
Fairy-ring fungi need open ground, which only the edge has
items.why: The fungus has used up the soil behind it and can only grow outward. It fruits where it is feeding and growing, which is the front.

items.ask: Two fairy rings grow into each other. What does Wollaston's idea predict?
choices: The older ring swallows the younger
items.why: Each fungus would have to grow into soil the other has already used. So neither can advance there, and the arcs where they touch fade out.

items.ask: Why is the grass often darker and thicker at the edge of a ring?
choices: The fungus frees nitrogen from the dead plant matter it digests
The fungus makes sugar that the grass absorbs
Mushrooms shade the grass and keep it moist
items.why: Digesting old roots and leaves releases the nitrogen in them as ammonium. Grass is often short of nitrogen, so it greens up where the fungus has just been.

items.ask: A ring is 30 metres across and spreads about 15 cm a year at its edge. About how old is it?
items.why: Its radius is 15 metres. At 0.15 metres a year, the edge took about 100 years to get there from the middle.

withering.title: Withering got there first
withering.text: Others before Wollaston, among them the botanist William Withering, the doctor who brought foxglove into medicine, had already suggested that fairy rings were made by fungi. Wollaston's paper went further: it explained why a ring is a ring, and why rings do not cross.

length.title: How much hypha in a gram?
length.text: Estimates vary a great deal with the soil and the method. Grassland soils hold metres to tens of metres of hyphae per gram; rich forest soils, with their root fungi, can hold far more. Laid end to end, the hyphae under one footstep in a forest might reach kilometres.

dry.title: Water-repellent soil
dry.text: Soil under a dense mycelium becomes hydrophobic: rain beads on it and runs off rather than soaking in. Greenkeepers deal with the dead bands on golf greens by spiking the turf and using wetting agents to get water back into it.

france.title: The largest rings
france.text: The ring near Belfort in France, made by the trooping funnel mushroom, is the one usually quoted, at about 600 metres across and perhaps 700 years old. Such figures come from the size and an assumed rate of spread, so they are rough; but a ring that wide could not be young.
